questions.stem: Light of photon energy \({{E}}\ \text{eV}\) falls on a metal of work function \({{phi}}\ \text{eV}\). The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is:

whyWrong.A: This is the full photon energy; part of it must be spent to free the electron.
whyWrong.B: Adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
whyWrong.D: This is the work function, the energy lost in escaping the surface, not the kinetic energy left over.

explanation.trapUsed: Sign trap: adding instead of subtracting the work function.
explanation.howToModify: Give the wavelength instead of the photon energy so the learner must first compute \(h c/\lambda\).
explanation.howToAvoid: Write energy conservation explicitly: photon energy = escape energy + kinetic energy.

questions.stem: In Compton scattering of X-rays by free electrons, the maximum possible wavelength shift is (\(\lambda_C = h/m_e c \approx 2.43\ \text{pm}\)):

options.B: zero, because the photon energy is conserved

whyWrong.A: At \(60^\circ\) the shift is \(\lambda_C/2\); again not the maximum.
whyWrong.B: The photon gives energy to the recoiling electron, so its energy (and wavelength) changes.
whyWrong.C: At \(90^\circ\) the shift is \(\lambda_C\), but this is not the maximum.

explanation.conceptTested: Compton shift formula and its angular dependence
explanation.trapUsed: Confusing the Compton wavelength with the maximum shift.
explanation.howToModify: Ask for the kinetic energy of the recoil electron at back-scattering for a given incident wavelength.
explanation.howToAvoid: Remember \(1-\cos\theta\) ranges from 0 to 2, so the shift ranges from 0 to \(2\lambda_C\).

questions.stem: An electron at rest is accelerated through a potential difference of \(100\ \text{V}\). Its de Broglie wavelength is approximately:

explanation.whyCorrect: \(\lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV} \approx 12.27/\sqrt{V}\ \text{Å}\). For \(V = 100\ \text{V}\), \(\lambda \approx 1.23\ \text{Å}\), comparable to atomic spacings — which is why electrons diffract from crystals.

whyWrong.C: Forgets to take the square root of 100 (divides by 1 instead of 10).
whyWrong.D: Off by a factor of 10 — divides by 100 instead of \(\sqrt{100}\).

explanation.conceptTested: de Broglie wavelength of an accelerated electron
explanation.howToModify: Use a proton or alpha particle instead of an electron, changing the mass and charge.
explanation.howToAvoid: Memorise \(\lambda_e \approx 12.27/\sqrt{V}\ \text{Å}\) and sanity-check: 100 V electrons have Å-scale wavelengths.

questions.stem: Which experiment first gave direct confirmation of the wave nature of electrons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Davisson and Germer (1927) observed diffraction maxima when electrons scattered from a nickel crystal, at angles matching the de Broglie wavelength.

whyWrong.A: Franck–Hertz showed quantized energy levels of atoms.
whyWrong.D: Stern–Gerlach demonstrated space quantization and electron spin.

explanation.howToModify: Ask which experiment confirmed quantized atomic energy levels (answer: Franck–Hertz).
explanation.howToAvoid: Link each experiment to the single property it proved: spin, levels, waves, charge.

questions.stem: The ultraviolet catastrophe of the Rayleigh–Jeans law was removed by Planck's assumption that:

options.A: equipartition holds for every mode at all frequencies
options.B: electromagnetic waves travel at speed \(c\) in every frame
options.C: the oscillators exchange energy only in discrete amounts \(nh\nu\)
options.D: the number of modes per unit frequency is independent of \(\nu\)

explanation.whyCorrect: Quantized energy exchange makes high-frequency modes (with \(h\nu \gg kT\)) exponentially unlikely to be excited, so the energy density falls to zero at high \(\nu\) instead of diverging.

whyWrong.A: Equipartition for every mode is exactly what causes the catastrophe.
whyWrong.B: That is a postulate of special relativity, unrelated to blackbody spectra.
whyWrong.D: The mode density grows as \(\nu^2\); Planck kept this result.

explanation.trapUsed: Offering the very assumption that causes the failure as a 'solution'.
explanation.howToModify: Ask in which limit Planck's law reduces to Rayleigh–Jeans (answer: \(h\nu \ll kT\)).
explanation.howToAvoid: Ask yourself: which assumption makes high-frequency modes cost a large energy step?

questions.stem: Monochromatic light above the threshold frequency falls on a photocathode. If the intensity is doubled while the frequency is kept fixed, then:

options.B: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles
options.D: the photocurrent roughly doubles while the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged

explanation.whyCorrect: Intensity at fixed frequency means more photons per second, each of the same energy. More photons free more electrons (larger current), but each electron still receives \(h\nu\), so \(K_{max}\) and the stopping potential are unchanged.

whyWrong.A: Threshold frequency is \(\phi/h\), a property of the metal.
whyWrong.B: This is the classical wave prediction that the photoelectric effect disproved.
whyWrong.C: Stopping potential measures \(K_{max}/e\), which depends only on frequency.

explanation.conceptTested: Intensity versus frequency in the photoelectric effect
explanation.trapUsed: Classical-wave intuition (brighter light gives faster electrons).
explanation.howToModify: Instead change the frequency at fixed intensity and ask what happens to the number of photons.
explanation.howToAvoid: Separate 'how many photons' (intensity) from 'energy per photon' (frequency).
